Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer effectively weaves together real-time scenes and compressed summaries to create an emotionally resonant narrative. The first three sections rely heavily on vivid scenes—eating breakfast, doing the crossword puzzle, driving to the post office, and playing gin rummy—using crisp dialogue and specific actions to bring the mother's stubborn, endearing personality and her relationship with her son to life. Interwoven into these scenes is concise exposition (such as the history of the house, the father's death, and the mother's habits) that provides necessary context without slowing the pace. Later in the story, the author appropriately uses summary to bridge a five-week gap and quickly convey the events of the mother's heatstroke and hospitalization, before returning to a quiet, reflective real-time scene as the son gathers her belongings from the empty house. This balance keeps the pacing smooth and maximizes the emotional impact of the ending.
